source_file: zhihu_面试时谈薪的技巧有些什么啊.txt

heuristics.rule: Always ask about compensation structure before stating your number
heuristics.condition: When entering the salary negotiation phase of an offer discussion...
heuristics.action: Ask about base salary structure, performance bonuses, supplements, social insurance contribution rates, and number of months paid before revealing your expectations
heuristics.because: The source explicitly warns against jumping straight to a number without understanding what you're comparing; a 12-month base at one company versus a 13-month base at another creates large differences that make raw monthly figures misleading

heuristics.rule: Report your expected salary (期望薪资), not your acceptable floor (底线薪资), as your opening number
heuristics.condition: When asked for your salary expectation in a first round...
heuristics.action: Quote your target number, leaving room for the recruiter to negotiate downward — never lead with your minimum
heuristics.because: The source states explicitly: 'report price should be expected salary, leaving HR room to bargain' — if you open at your floor there is no room left

heuristics.rule: Use a competing offer (real or imminent) as leverage only after the recruiter has shown they want you
heuristics.condition: When the recruiter has made an offer below your target and signaled strong interest in you...
heuristics.action: Mention the competing offer without naming the company, express preference for the current employer, and ask for a specific number you would accept
heuristics.because: The case study in the source shows this sequence worked: candidate disclosed competing offer at 37k, expressed preference for current company, asked for 36k specifically, and got it via special approval

heuristics.rule: Prepare written documentation of every component of current compensation before negotiations begin
heuristics.condition: When preparing to negotiate a job change...
heuristics.action: Compile a spreadsheet covering monthly base, number of months, all supplements (meal, transport, housing), bonuses for the last 3 years, equity, and benefits — with proof for each line item
heuristics.because: The source's Case A shows that failing to communicate full comp upfront leads to an awkward post-offer renegotiation that damages trust and risks losing the offer entirely

heuristics.rule: Counter HR's 'maximum raise is 10%' by reframing the base, not fighting the percentage
heuristics.condition: When HR claims a company policy caps raises at a fixed percentage...
heuristics.action: Argue that the correct base to apply the percentage to is your market-adjusted or soon-to-be-adjusted salary, not your current depressed salary
heuristics.because: The source provides explicit sample language: 'using last month's salary with a 10% raise to assess my current experience and ability is not reasonable'

heuristics.rule: Treat verbal promises of future raises, stock options, or growth opportunities as non-binding and exclude them from base salary negotiation
heuristics.condition: When a recruiter pivots to equity, future raises, or 'great growth opportunities' to justify a lower base...
heuristics.action: Acknowledge the upside, then redirect: 'those represent future value I create; right now we're agreeing on what my current experience is worth'
heuristics.because: The source explicitly categorizes all such items as '各种各样的饼（全都是泡沫）' and provides scripts to deflect them

heuristics.rule: Watch for hedging language from HR as a signal that the offer is negotiable
heuristics.condition: When HR says phrases like 'normally...', 'generally speaking...', 'I'll need to check on that', or 'let me ask internally'...
heuristics.action: Take this as confirmation that flexibility exists and push harder for your target number
heuristics.because: The source explicitly lists these phrases as signals that 'the company's compensation is elastically adjustable'

heuristics.rule: If your bonus history is volatile, present a multi-year average as your compensation base
heuristics.condition: When your most recent year had an unusually low bonus that would make your total comp appear artificially low...
heuristics.action: Provide a 3-year average with supporting bank statements, and negotiate the new offer against that average
heuristics.because: Case B in the source shows a candidate got 8% above the 3-year average — more than 15% above last year's actual — by presenting the multi-year data proactively

decision_factors.why_it_matters: The higher the match, the more leverage the candidate has — a weak match means the employer can easily look at other candidates if the negotiation stalls
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Honestly map your actual experience against each listed job requirement; the source suggests 80%+ match as the threshold for aggressive negotiation

decision_factors.factor: Company urgency to fill the role
decision_factors.why_it_matters: A company that is actively understaffed will approve higher-than-normal offers to close quickly; a company recruiting speculatively will not
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Research via professional networks (e.g., 脉脉) to see how long the role has been open and whether the team is visibly short-handed

decision_factors.factor: Whether you hold at least one other competing offer
decision_factors.why_it_matters: A real competing offer transforms negotiation from 'please give me more' to 'I have alternatives' — it shifts power and creates genuine urgency for the recruiter
decision_factors.how_to_assess: The source advises not to negotiate aggressively on your first-ever offer if you have no backup; wait until you have a baseline offer before pushing hard at any single employer

decision_factors.factor: Compensation structure differences between old and new employer
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Direct monthly salary comparisons are misleading when one employer pays 12 months and the other pays 13, or one provides housing while the other does not
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Convert all compensation to a single annual total-comp number before comparing; monetize non-cash benefits at market rates

decision_factors.factor: HR's actual authority level vs. stated authority
decision_factors.why_it_matters: HR often claims a ceiling that is actually their personal approval limit, not the true maximum — a strong candidate can trigger a special approval process above that limit
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Watch for hedging phrases; ask whether a special exception process exists; reference the recruiter's interest in closing to motivate them to escalate

decision_factors.factor: Gap between current salary and market rate for the role
decision_factors.why_it_matters: If your current salary is significantly below market, using it as the negotiation base disadvantages you; framing the ask around market rate is more defensible
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check job boards and salary tools for the same title, years of experience, and city; document the gap explicitly

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Leaving compensation details vague during early recruiter calls to avoid 'anchoring low'
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: After the offer is issued, trying to add overlooked components (13th month, meal stipend, housing benefit) feels like bad faith to the recruiter and can collapse the deal entirely
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who are disorganized about their own compensation or who assume the recruiter will figure it out

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a salary figure that seems like a 20–30% raise over monthly base
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The raise disappears or reverses when the new company pays 12 months vs. 13, has lower bonus averages, lower social insurance contributions, or removes non-monetary benefits like subsidized housing or meal cards
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who compare only headline monthly base figures without converting to total annual compensation

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating purely on base salary while ignoring bonus structure
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: At companies where bonus is a large share of total comp, winning a higher base but accepting a lower expected bonus can result in lower total comp than an alternative offer with lower base but reliable bonus
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates at companies or levels where bonus is material (finance, tech, senior roles)

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Verbally accepting or strongly signaling acceptance before clarifying all terms
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Once the recruiter believes the deal is done, they lose motivation to re-open any aspect of it; asking to adjust afterward is perceived as reneging and damages the relationship
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Candidates who are conflict-averse and signal agreement prematurely to avoid tension

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying on verbal promises about future salary increases or performance bonuses as part of the total package
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Verbal commitments are unenforceable; the source explicitly flags that year-end bonuses paid in June of the following year, discretionary raises, and unwritten equity grants may never materialize
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: First-time job changers or anyone joining a company without verifying what is written into the contract

failure_patterns.pattern: Giving a vague salary range instead of a specific number
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates fear commitment and hope flexibility will help them; they anchor low with the floor of their range without realizing it
failure_patterns.consequence: Recruiter anchors to the low end of the range; candidate feels underpaid but has no grounds to push back since they gave the number

failure_patterns.pattern: Failing to document all components of current compensation before negotiating
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates know their monthly take-home intuitively but have never summed the full package; they assume the recruiter will ask follow-up questions
failure_patterns.consequence: Post-offer renegotiation attempts look dishonest and damage trust; the recruiter may move to the second-choice candidate rather than re-open the approval process
warning_signs: Can only quote monthly base when asked about compensation
Has never computed annual total comp including bonuses and benefits

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting HR's framing that 'maximum raise is X%' as a fixed constraint
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The policy sounds official and candidates feel they have no standing to challenge a stated company rule
failure_patterns.consequence: Candidate leaves money on the table; the real ceiling (with special approval) was higher, but candidate never triggered the escalation process
warning_signs: Immediately accepting the first number after HR mentions a policy
Not asking whether exceptions or special approvals exist

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating future equity, bonuses, and growth opportunities as equivalent to current base salary in negotiations
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: HR actively promotes these as substitutes; candidates are susceptible to optimistic narratives, especially at growing companies
failure_patterns.consequence: Candidate accepts a lower base on the strength of uncertain future payouts that may never arrive; they are locked into the lower base for all future raise calculations
warning_signs: Feeling satisfied after recruiter mentions 'great stock options'
Mentally adding unconfirmed bonus to base to reach a target number

failure_patterns.pattern: Negotiating without a competing offer or any leverage when market conditions are weak
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates feel pressure to close quickly in a tough job market and overestimate their negotiating position
failure_patterns.consequence: Pushing too hard without leverage leads to offer rescission or the recruiter turning to other candidates; candidate ends up with nothing
warning_signs: Long job search with no other offers pending
Candidate has told the recruiter they have no other options

failure_patterns.pattern: Inflating or fabricating salary history to anchor the negotiation higher
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates believe they can get away with unverifiable claims; they want to establish a higher baseline
failure_patterns.consequence: Employers increasingly cross-check via bank statements, tax records, and background checks; fabrication can result in offer rescission, contract termination, and industry blacklisting
warning_signs: Candidate is slow or evasive when asked for salary proof
Stated salary is inconsistent across documents

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have at least one other offer at or near your target number?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether you have real leverage or are negotiating from pure desire
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Use the competing offer as a reference point; express preference for this employer and ask for a specific number you would accept to close
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Build leverage through match quality and company urgency arguments rather than competing offers; avoid aggressive tactics that could kill the deal

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you converted your current total compensation to a single annual number including all components?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether you can make an apples-to-apples comparison with the new offer
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Use that number as your negotiation anchor and document each component with proof
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Stop and build the full picture before entering any salary discussion; missing components discovered post-offer create damaging renegotiations

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the compensation structure of the new company — how many months of base, how is bonus calculated, what benefits are included?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the headline monthly number is directly comparable to your current comp or requires adjustment
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If structure is known, recalculate both sides on the same basis before setting your target number
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Ask these questions before revealing your number; the source provides exact scripts for this inquiry

diagnostic_questions.question: How well do you match the specific requirements of this role, honestly assessed?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: How much negotiating leverage you actually have — a high-match candidate is harder to replace, giving them more room to push
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If match is 80%+, negotiate assertively and invoke match quality as a reason for the premium
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If match is below 70%, prioritize getting the offer over maximizing the number; aggressive negotiation risks losing the offer to a better-matched candidate

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the HR representative using hedging language like 'normally', 'generally', or 'I'll need to check'?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the stated compensation ceiling is a hard limit or a soft starting position
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Push for a specific number above their initial offer and ask them to escalate internally
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If language is firm and definitive, assess whether the gap between offer and expectation is worth risking the deal

industry_realities.common_belief: HR's stated maximum salary or raise cap is a fixed company policy that cannot be exceeded
industry_realities.actual_reality: HR often has a personal approval limit below the true ceiling; exceeding it requires going to a higher manager for special approval, which HR will do if the candidate is strong enough and they are motivated to close
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should not accept HR's first ceiling as final — they should give HR the motivation and supporting evidence to escalate by making the case for their own value clearly

industry_realities.common_belief: The right time to discuss salary expectations is at the formal offer stage
industry_realities.actual_reality: Recruiters and headhunters begin forming compensation expectations from the very first contact; questions about current salary and job-change motivation in the first call are already part of the compensation negotiation
industry_realities.implication: Candidates must have their full compensation picture ready from the first recruiter call, not just when the formal offer arrives

industry_realities.actual_reality: As of recent years (2024–2025 based on context), the market for successful negotiated increases has compressed to 10–15% in many industries; 20–30% is achievable but requires strong leverage
industry_realities.implication: Candidates anchoring their expectations to the old 20–30% norm may need to adjust targets or accept that they need unusually strong leverage to achieve it

industry_realities.common_belief: Once an offer is issued in writing, the negotiation is over
industry_realities.actual_reality: A written offer can still be renegotiated if done quickly and professionally, but it is significantly harder — the recruiter must restart the approval process, which they are reluctant to do
industry_realities.implication: All clarifications and counter-requests should be made before the offer is formally issued, not after

industry_realities.common_belief: Mentioning a competing offer is risky and may offend the recruiter
industry_realities.actual_reality: A real competing offer at or above your target is one of the most effective pieces of leverage available; experienced recruiters expect it and respond to it by seeking special approval
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should not hide competing offers out of politeness; they should disclose them strategically while expressing genuine preference for the current employer to avoid appearing mercenary

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How they respond when asked their salary expectation
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Gives a vague range ('5k to 10k is fine') or says 'I trust the company to give me a fair number'
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: States a specific number grounded in documented current comp plus a justified market-rate adjustment, and can explain the logic component by component
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A vague answer anchors the negotiation at the low end; an informed specific ask anchors it at the right level and signals competence

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How they handle HR's 'we can only do X% raise' response
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Accepts the constraint and tries to negotiate within the stated percentage
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Challenges the base the percentage is applied to — argues that current salary is below market or that an upcoming internal raise should be the true base
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Accepting the percentage framing means fighting over small dollars; reframing the base can result in thousands more even at the same percentage

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How they treat future bonuses, equity, and growth promises during negotiation
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Mentally counts verbal promises as part of the package and reduces their base salary ask accordingly
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Explicitly separates current base from future and uncertain elements; negotiates each independently and insists that promises be written into the contract
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Verbal upside that never materializes leaves the candidate locked into a lower base with no recourse

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Preparation before the first recruiter call
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Thinks about salary only when asked; knows their monthly take-home but not their full annual comp
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Has already built a full compensation spreadsheet with every component documented and proof materials ready to send within minutes
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Being caught unprepared forces improvisation; improvisation leads to underquoting, overlooked components, and post-offer renegotiations that damage trust

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Waits for the 'salary negotiation phase' and treats early recruiter calls as purely informational
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Understands that compensation positioning begins at first contact and treats every question about current salary as part of the negotiation
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: By the time a formal offer is made, the recruiter has already formed a comp ceiling based on what the candidate communicated earlier; late corrections are much harder

community_misconceptions.misconception: HR will give you a fair salary if you trust the process — no need to negotiate aggressively
community_misconceptions.why_believed: It feels confrontational to push back; many candidates want to appear agreeable and assume companies act in good faith on compensation
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: HR is optimizing for the company's budget, not the candidate's wellbeing; the opening offer almost always has negotiation room built in
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Candidates who don't negotiate leave 20–60% of achievable compensation on the table, according to the source

community_misconceptions.misconception: Giving a wide salary range is safer because it gives you flexibility
community_misconceptions.why_believed: A range feels less committal and candidates think it avoids conflict while still conveying their general expectations
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Recruiters anchor to the bottom of any range you give; a range signals indecision and gives the employer a free anchor at your minimum
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Candidate gets offered the floor of their stated range or lower, having anchored the negotiation against themselves

community_misconceptions.misconception: You can negotiate salary only at the formal offer stage
community_misconceptions.why_believed: The offer stage feels like the 'official' moment for compensation discussion; earlier conversations feel premature
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Compensation framing begins at the first recruiter call when they ask about current salary and job-change motivation; the formal offer stage just confirms what was already established
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Candidates who don't manage the comp framing early find the recruiter has already anchored internally to a number, making later negotiation much harder

community_misconceptions.misconception: HR's stated salary ceiling or raise-cap policy is a hard limit you cannot exceed
community_misconceptions.why_believed: The phrasing 'company policy' sounds official and non-negotiable; candidates don't want to appear unreasonable by challenging a stated rule
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: HR's stated ceiling is often their personal approval authority, not the company's true maximum; strong candidates can trigger a special approval process
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Candidates accept a below-potential offer when a special approval would have yielded their target number

community_misconceptions.misconception: Inflating your salary history slightly is a safe way to get a higher offer since it's hard to verify
community_misconceptions.why_believed: In the past, salary verification was rare; candidates assume the recruiter takes their word for it
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Employers increasingly require bank statements, tax records, and original offer letters; background checks include HR-to-HR salary verification calls
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Fabrication is discoverable; if caught it results in offer rescission, contract termination, and potential industry blacklisting

real_case_outcomes.situation: Candidate (小王) negotiated salary without disclosing full compensation details upfront; failed to mention 13th-month salary and various supplements during initial call
real_case_outcomes.decision: Let the recruiter issue an offer based on incomplete information, then tried to raise the 13th month, meal stipend, and transport allowance after the written offer was issued
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Recruiter became frustrated, offer re-approval was burdensome, recruiter began considering second-choice candidate; deal stalled with neither party advancing it
real_case_outcomes.lesson: All compensation components must be communicated proactively before the offer is issued — post-offer discovery attempts are perceived as bad faith and can kill the deal

real_case_outcomes.situation: Same candidate (小王, improved version) prepared a full compensation breakdown including 13th month, 3-year bonus average, and imminent pay raise; disclosed a competing offer during negotiations
real_case_outcomes.decision: Presented documented comp total of ~430k/year, argued for 55k/year target based on upcoming raise as base; later disclosed a competing offer at target level and expressed genuine preference for current company; asked for specific number (36k/month) to close
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Recruiter escalated to special approval process with hiring manager; candidate received 36k/month offer, above the initially stated ceiling of 35k
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Documented comp history, a competing offer, and a specific closing ask (not a range) together can unlock special approval processes that exceed stated HR ceilings

real_case_outcomes.situation: Candidate (小陈) had a volatile bonus history — 1 month last year but 4 months average the two prior years
real_case_outcomes.decision: Headhunter presented a 3-year average compensation figure with supporting bank statements, requesting 10% above that average
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Employer offered 8% above the 3-year average — lower than the 10% ask but substantially higher than 15% above last year's actual comp would have produced
real_case_outcomes.lesson: When recent comp is anomalously low, anchoring the negotiation to a documented multi-year average is more effective than fighting over a percentage of the bad year

real_case_outcomes.situation: Friend of poster received initial max offer of 10k vs. expected 14k; company had pressing hiring need and candidate had 4+ years relevant experience with 80%+ role match
real_case_outcomes.decision: Candidate itemized specific differentials between old and new company benefits (social insurance contribution levels, absence of overtime pay), then mentioned a competing offer to create urgency
real_case_outcomes.outcome: HR called the next day and confirmed 14k offer had been approved
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Concrete benefit-differential arguments combined with competing offer leverage are more effective than simply restating a desired number; the combination triggers HR escalation

psychological_barriers.trigger: Candidate says 'HR already said the maximum is X, I don't think it's possible to negotiate further'
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Authority deference — treating an institutional-sounding statement as immovable fact; fear of appearing difficult or unreasonable
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Candidate immediately accepts stated ceiling, abandons negotiation, and either accepts a below-market offer or walks away without trying
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe HR's ceiling as their personal authority limit, not the company's true maximum; explain that a strong candidate case gives HR the ammunition to escalate — your job is to provide that ammunition

psychological_barriers.trigger: Candidate says 'the job market is bad right now, I should just take what they give me'
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Scarcity mindset and catastrophizing — overweighting the risk of losing the offer relative to the benefit of negotiating
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Candidate accepts the first offer without negotiating, even when the company clearly needs them and has flexibility
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Point out that by the offer stage the company has already invested significantly in the candidate; the cost of restarting the search is real for them too — the candidate has more leverage than they feel they do

psychological_barriers.trigger: Candidate feels excitement and relief at receiving an offer and wants to close quickly to avoid risking it
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Loss aversion activated by finally having an offer in hand — fear that any push-back will cause the offer to be rescinded
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Candidate accepts immediately without counter-offering, or makes a token counter well below their actual target
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Normalize the expectation that negotiation is standard and expected; a well-framed counter virtually never results in offer rescission — recruiters build in buffer precisely because they expect negotiation

psychological_barriers.trigger: Candidate receives an offer below their target and asks 'should I just accept? I don't want to rock the boat'
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Conflict avoidance — discomfort with assertiveness framed as pragmatism
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Candidate frames accepting a below-target offer as 'being realistic' rather than acknowledging they are avoiding a difficult conversation
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Separate the emotional discomfort from the financial stakes; provide a script so the candidate only needs to repeat prepared language rather than improvise under pressure

psychological_barriers.trigger: Candidate hesitates to mention a competing offer because it 'feels dishonest' or 'too aggressive'
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Social norm violation anxiety — fear that using leverage will be perceived as manipulative or will damage the relationship with the recruiter
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Candidate withholds their strongest piece of leverage out of politeness, leaving thousands on the table
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Frame competing offers as market information, not threats — 'I want to be transparent that I'm evaluating another opportunity, and I'd prefer to be here, but I need the numbers to make sense'

reframing_moves.original_framing: 'My current salary is low, so I don't deserve a big raise' or 'HR is using my current salary as the baseline'
reframing_moves.reframe: Your current salary reflects what you were worth when you joined that company years ago — it does not reflect what your current experience is worth on the market today
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Separates historical accident (underpaid entry) from current market value; shifts the anchor from a number that disadvantages the candidate to one grounded in what the role actually requires
reframing_moves.example_language: 'My current salary reflects my compensation 3 years ago when I joined; my growth since then is not captured in that number, and it is already below market average'

reframing_moves.original_framing: 'They promised good bonuses and growth opportunities, so maybe the lower base is okay'
reframing_moves.reframe: Future bonuses are future value you will create then — they are a separate question from what your current experience is worth today
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Forces a clean separation between present compensation for present skills versus future compensation for future performance; prevents the candidate from discounting certain present-value dollars for uncertain future ones
reframing_moves.example_language: 'Future raises represent the extra value I create after I join; what we're negotiating now is what my existing experience is worth — those are two different questions'

reframing_moves.original_framing: 'The company's policy is a maximum 10% raise, so I can only push within that range'
reframing_moves.reframe: The percentage is not the constraint — the base the percentage is applied to is the constraint; change the base and the same percentage yields a very different number
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Breaks the false assumption that accepting the percentage framing means accepting the employer's preferred base; opens up a new axis of negotiation
reframing_moves.example_language: 'If we apply 10% to my salary as it will be after next month's internal adjustment, the number looks quite different from applying it to today's below-market figure'

reframing_moves.original_framing: 'I need to convince HR to give me more money'
reframing_moves.reframe: You need to give HR the ammunition to go to their manager and fight for you — your job is to make their internal case as easy as possible
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Shifts the candidate from an adversarial 'demanding' posture to a collaborative 'enabling' posture; aligns the candidate's interest with the recruiter's interest in closing the deal
reframing_moves.example_language: 'Here is the documentation of my current comp and market data — I hope this gives you what you need to make the case internally'

reframing_moves.original_framing: 'I should ask for a range to seem flexible and reasonable'
reframing_moves.reframe: Giving a range means you have already named your floor — the recruiter will anchor to it and call it your expectation
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Reveals the hidden cost of appearing 'flexible'; transforms the candidate's instinct for politeness into a concrete numerical disadvantage they can see clearly
reframing_moves.example_language: 'A range just tells them the lowest number you'll accept — give them one number, the right one'
